extracted.intended_audience: general public, science communicators, journalists, and early-career researchers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for members of the public and science communicators on how to evaluate scientific claims in media and to press for transparency (especially whether findings have been peer reviewed). Encourages journalists and scientists to disclose sources and engage the public clearly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demand disclosure of peer review status
rubrics_metrics.description: Demand that anyone providing 'scientific' results reveal whether those results have been peer reviewed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The peer review system can help cut through uncertainty and obfuscation; Sense about Science's Ask for Evidence campaign prompts people to ask providers to reveal whether results have been peer reviewed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask for evidence / question scientific-sounding information
rubrics_metrics.description: Prompt people to question scientific-sounding information rather than accepting claims at face value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Ask for Evidence campaign encourages the public to ask for evidence behind claims; Sense about Science held boot camps and a Voice of Young Science program to plan ways to spread this behavior nationwide. Targeted topics included dietary supplements, gun control policy, fracking, changing weather patterns, 'superfoods', vaccinations, alternative medicine and radiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include citations of published papers in news stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists should include citations of published papers when reporting scientific findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The BBC instated an official policy that all of its online reporters should include citations of published papers in their stories; this practice helps readers judge the source and credibility of claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: State the source of research and name the journal if published
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting new research, state where the research has come from and name the journal if the work has been published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most British newspapers now state where new research has come from, and if the work has been published they will name the journal — a transparency practice the article contrasts with lagging American media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide explanatory guides that teach how scientists present and judge information (including peer review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Educational materials for the public should explain how scientists present and judge information, including the role and meaning of peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sense about Science's guide 'I Don’t Know What to Believe: Making Sense of Science Stories' explains these topics and is used by health workers, librarians, public-health officials, policy-makers, technology companies, safety bodies, popular writers, educators, parenting groups and local governments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage scientists (including early-career) to speak clearly and engage the public
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientists should speak up clearly in public debates so non-specialists have a chance of making sense of science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Voice of Young Science program encourages early career researchers to play an active role in public debates; John Durant urged scientists of all ages to speak out more and clearly to ensure they're heard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Challenge those who spin or misuse scientific facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Public-facing programs should actively challenge hucksters, charlatans and advocates who spin facts for selfish use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such challenges provide an important public service by helping people make more informed and intelligent judgments about their health and well-being, as noted by risk-communication experts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design campaigns to raise public awareness and measurable understanding of peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Public-awareness campaigns should aim to increase understanding of peer review (e.g., showing many Brits can explain the system after outreach).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sense about Science's decade-long U.K. work led to many people being able to explain peer review when asked; campaigns can replicate that effect through guides, media practices, and outreach.
